title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling & runbooks
author: Ethan Park
content:
Summary
-------
This document consolidates the serving runtime reference: architecture, kernel scheduling policies, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, release note guidance, a concise known-issues catalogue, and operational runbooks. It is intended for engineers on serving-runtime, infra, and SRE who operate or change the inference runtime.

Goals & scope
- Provide a single-page reference for runtime design and operational runbooks.
- Describe deterministic kernel selection and scheduling policies used in production.
- Capture profiling steps and tooling to reproduce regressions locally and in CI.
- Document the benchmarking matrix and how to add new workloads.
- Standardize release notes and incident remediation steps.

Ownership and SLAs
- Owner team: engineering (serving-runtime). Primary oncall: serving-runtime team.
- SLOs (global): 99.9% availability; latency targets vary by model class – typical P95 text-gen <= 250ms on Dedicated for short contexts (<= 128 tokens).
- Alerts: P95 latency > target for 5m; 5% error rate sustained for 3m; GPU memory pressure > 85% for 1m.

Architecture overview
- Component diagram (textual):
  1) Frontend API layer (http/gRPC) — request validation, auth, tenant quotas.
  2) Router & policy engine — routes requests to capacity pools (hosted/dedicated/private) and compatible model variants.
  3) Scheduler / batching service — forms micro-batches; enforces latency SLOs and priority tiers.
  4) Kernel selector / runtime executor — chooses optimized kernels (cuBLAS/cuDNN/custom CUDA kernels) based on model, sequence length, quantization.
  5) Worker process (per-GPU) — manages KV cache, attention state, and per-request token emission.
  6) Observability layer — tracing, metrics (Prometheus), and streaming logs.
  7) Persistence & config — model artifacts, quantization profiles, kernel registry.

Key design notes
- Continuous batching: scheduler balances increased throughput with latency SLOs by bounding batch sizes per latency budget.
- KV caching: prefix caching at tenant granularity; shared-read caches for commonly requested prompts.
- Kernel registry: deterministic mapping from (model_family, dtype, seq_len_range, hardware_capability) -> kernel_variant.
- Fallbacks: fallback to FP16/INT8 variants if preferred kernels unavailable, with quality warnings and throttling to preserve availability.

Kernel scheduling policy (detailed)
- Priority tiers:
  - P0 (system/internal): healthchecks, control plane traffic — preemptive, highest priority.
  - P1 (interactive): low-latency customer requests (default SLA).
  - P2 (batch/async): background evals, large-batch offline jobs.
- Scheduling algorithm:
  1) Admission control: checks tenant quotas, model compatibility, and current GPU pressure.
  2) Batching decision: per-GPU adaptive batch size computed from target latency and recent latency percentiles.
  3) Kernel variant selection: choose kernel with best historical throughput for the (seq_len, dtype) bucket; if not available, pick nearest compatible variant.
  4) Preemption: P0/P1 can preempt P2 batches using cooperative eviction (finish in-flight tokens up to safe boundary).
- Affinity & placement rules:
  - Warm affinity: keep requests for pinned model versions on same worker to preserve KV cache hit rate.
  - NUMA/GPU affinity: prefer intra-node placement to avoid NVLink contention for multi-GPU models.
- Safety knobs (configurable via runtime flags):
  - max_batch_size: integer
  - latency_target_ms: integer
  - preemptive_threshold: percent GPU occupancy to enable aggressive preemption
  - kernel_selection_policy: ["throughput_first", "latency_first", "cost_aware"]

Profiling playbook (how-to reproduce and triage performance regressions)
- When to profile:
  - Sudden P95/P99 latency increase on a model route.
  - Throughput drop with unchanged request pattern.
  - Regressions detected by CI benchmark suite.
- Tools & traces:
  - Tracing: Jaeger (span annotations for scheduler, kernel_select, execution_start/stop).
  - System profilers: nvidia-smi, nvprof / Nsight Systems, perf, hwloc.
  - Application-level: torch.profiler (if model uses PyTorch kernels), custom runtime tracing (runtimetrace CLI).
- Step-by-step profiling guide:
  1) Capture distributed traces for a 10–15 minute window surrounding the incident.
  2) Correlate trace spans with Prometheus metrics (GPU_util, batch_size, kv_cache_hit).
  3) Run a controlled reproduce on a staging worker with representative input. Use the benchmark harness (see Benchmarking suite) and enable kernel tracing.
  4) Collect a GPU timeline with Nsight Systems: nv-nsight-cli --capture-range -o nsight_report.qns
  5) Inspect kernel durations and occupancy. If kernels show serialization or long host-to-device memcpy, inspect batching and prefetch logic.
  6) For memory issues, use cuda-memcheck and analyze alloc/free patterns.
  7) Create a perf flamegraph of the runtime to find CPU-side scheduling hotspots (e.g., locks in the batching queue).
- Common root causes and checks:
  - Reduced KV cache hit rate -> cold cache or eviction bug. Check tenant affinity logs.
  - Kernel fallback to slower variant -> check kernel_registry and kernel_selection logs.
  - NVLink saturation from cross-GPU comms -> check per-GPU interconnect metrics.

Benchmarking suite (how to run & add workloads)
- Purpose: provide reproducible throughput/latency baselines across hardware and kernel variants.
- Benchmark matrix columns: model_name, model_size (params), dtype (fp16/int8), seq_len, batch_sizes, hardware (A100-40GB, A100-80GB, H100), kernel_variant, measured_P50_ms, measured_P95_ms, tokens_per_second.
- Running the suite (short):
  1) Checkout repo: git clone git@repo:redwood/serving-benchmarks.git
  2) Prepare model artifacts and quantization profiles in /bench-data.
  3) Start harness: ./bench-runner --model <model> --dtype fp16 --seq-len 128 --hardware a100-80 --duration 300 --collect-trace
  4) Results are pushed to /bench-results/<date>/<model>/<hardware>/summary.json and to bench-dashboard.
- Adding new workload:
  1) Add workload YAML to workloads/ with keys: name, model_uri, seq_len_ranges, dtype_options, sample_inputs.
  2) Add expected_quality_thresholds and cost_budget.
  3) Run bench-runner locally and submit PR with benchmark output and dashboards links.

Release notes template (runtime changes)
- Title: [serving-runtime] <short summary> (version X.Y.Z)
- Summary: 2–3 sentence summary of behavioral changes and reasons.
- Impact: list of affected customers, routes, or model families.
- Rollout plan: canary -> regional -> global with rollout percentages and health checks.
- Metrics to watch: latency P95/P99, KV cache hit rate, kernel_fallback_rate, GPU_util.
- Rollback instructions: how to pin to prior kernel registry or model variant.

Known issues (current, short catalog)
- ISSUE-2026-107: intermittent P99 spikes for seq_len 2048 on MPT-family models. Symptom: increased kernel_fallback_rate to legacy kernel. Mitigation: pin kernel_variant "mpt-opt-v2" until patch; temporary routing to dedicated pool with aggressive batching.
- ISSUE-2026-113: GPU OOM when serving quantized INT8 models with dynamic prompt expansion. Symptom: worker OOMs under long-context prompts. Mitigation: enforce max_context_tokens=4096 per-request at router; deploy memory-safety patch in runtime-v1.3.2.
- ISSUE-2026-121: NVLink throughput drops after driver update. Symptom: cross-GPU allreduce slower by 30%. Mitigation: Reboot driver and roll fleet staggered; upgrade CUDA driver to validated version.

Runbooks (incidents and ops playbooks)
- High-latency P95/P99 incident (quick runbook):
  1) Pager triggers to oncall owner.
  2) Confirm alert: check bench-dashboard and traces for the route.
  3) Identify scope: single worker / node / entire pool.
  4) If single worker: drain traffic (set weight=0), restart worker, collect nsight timeline, redeploy if needed.
  5) If pool-wide: scale up dedicated capacity, enable fallback routing to compatible model variant, open incident and communication with customers.
  6) Postmortem: capture root cause, regression test, and required change to bench-suite.
- OOM or memory pressure:
  1) Identify offending tenant and route with tooling (oom-tracker logs).
  2) Temporarily throttle large-context requests for that tenant.
  3) Rotate worker process, gather cuda-memcheck logs.
  4) Deploy memory fix or increase per-worker memory limit.
- Kernel regression detected in CI:
  1) Reproduce with bench-runner under deterministic RNG seed.
  2) Capture kernel selection logs and compare with golden registry.
  3) If kernel variant produces lower throughput, rollback kernel_registry entry and notify release owner.

Team wiki & references
- Confluence pages: see related_pages for operational playbooks and architecture ADRs.
- Important repos: git@repo:redwood/serving-runtime, git@repo:redwood/serving-benchmarks, git@repo:redwood/kernel-registry.
- Dashboards: bench-dashboard, runtime-health, kernel-variant-monitor.

Appendix: useful commands & config snippets
- Check GPU utilization (short): nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,memory.used --format=csv -l 2
- Collect Nsight trace (example): nv-nsight-cu-cli --export ./trace.qns --target-pid <worker_pid> --duration 60s
- Example kernel selection config (YAML):
  kernel_selection_policy: "latency_first"
  seq_len_buckets: [64,128,256,512,1024,2048]
  variant_preferences:
    mpt: ["mpt-opt-v2","mpt-opt-v1"]

- Example alert thresholds (Prometheus style):
  - expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, route)) > 0.25  # P95 > 250ms
  - expr: increase(runtime_worker_oom_total[5m]) > 0

Revision history
- 2026-02-15: created by Ethan Park (initial consolidated playbook).
- 2026-06-12: added kernel registry guidance and preemption semantics (review: Priya Nair).
- 2026-12-01: updated known issues and added CI bench-runner troubleshooting (review: Lucas Rivera).

If you are debugging an active incident and need help, @oncall-serving-runtime is the fastest contact. For process changes (scheduling policies, kernel defaults) open an ADR in /confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records and notify the owners listed above.
